title: Lightweight LLM synthesis: notes and next steps
body:
Quick context: scratchpad for 3 short papers + one systems talk I skimmed at Systems for ML 2027. Goal: extract actionable ideas we could prototype in Redwood Private for low-latency, low-cost edge-like inference (short queries, long contexts).

1) Sparse-KV-Mem (arXiv 2704.12345) — TL;DR: decompose KV cache into hot shards and cold shards; maintain a tiny LRU hot index in GPU DRAM, spill cold to device-local NVMe and fetch async.
  - Interesting: asynchronous prefetcher uses sequence prefix fingerprint to predict which cold shards will be needed for next tokens.
  - Notes: could map to our prefix caching layer; we already have simple KV cache eviction by recency, but not predictive prefetch.
  - Questions: prediction model size vs benefit? latency tail added by NVMe misses?
  - Quick experiment idea: implement a tiny predictor (hash-based + 1-layer MLP) in Python, run on replay of 10k traces from hosted API logs and measure prefetch hit growth.

2) Lowbit-Quant-Drift (blog post, May 2027) — TL;DR: 4-bit post-training quantization with calibration on short prompt subsets reduces drift for few-shot tasks if you keep first N layers in FP16.
  - Note: their heuristic kept first 3 transformer blocks FP16 for 7B models; for our models maybe 2 blocks enough.
  - Action: add a quantization profile to Optimize that suggests hybrid quant (head layers FP16) for short-response workloads. Add small eval harness in Optimize to score degradation on a few-shot prompt bank.

3) Prefix-compression-for-cache (conference poster) — TL;DR: compress repeated prefix KV entries via delta-encoding and bloom filters; reduces memory by ~30% for dialog workloads.
  - Implementation risk moderate (added CPU cycle to decompress during lookup). Benefit high for Dedicated where memory is scarce.
  - Suggestion: prototype server-side microbenchmark: compress LRU entries and measure lookup overhead under typical qps.

4) Panel notes (SfML 2027: productionizing ML systems) — main takeaway: engineering organizations prefer small, deterministic knobs (cache size, fallback model, batch window) vs complex heuristics. Ops wants transparency.
  - Translate to product: expose a simple slider in Console: "prefetch aggressiveness" + an "estimated extra tails ms" tooltip and cost delta.

To-dos / next actions (prioritized):
  - [P0] Run prefetch predictor replay: grab 10k request traces from hosted-api (privacy scrubbed), implement toy predictor, report hit-rate improvement. Owner: Kai. Due: 2027-06-09.
  - [P1] Add hybrid-quant profile to Optimize (low-effort): create eval set of 50 few-shot prompts, run quant variants, produce a recommendation template. Owner: Rita. Due: 2027-06-16.
  - [P2] Microbenchmark prefix-compression on Dedicated runtime: small C++/Rust bench to measure lookup overhead. Owner: Leah. Due: 2027-06-30.

Open questions / things to think about:
  - What telemetry do we need to estimate "cost delta" for prefetch aggressiveness? (per-token compute, NVMe IOPS cost, tail ms).
  - How to present hybrid-quant tradeoffs non-technically in Console? (samples: accuracy delta, expected inference cost %).
  - For Private customers, are we allowed to ship a predictor that trains on local traces? (privacy/legal).

Random scribbles:
  - If predictive prefetch uses fingerprint of prefix tokens, we can fold into routing metadata so dedicated pools can pre-warm caches before a request arrives. Useful for bursty chatbots.
  - Might reuse existing rollout infra: canary new prefetch model on <1% of traffic and monitor tail latencies + hallucination rate.

Useful links / bookmarks copied here for later:
  - arXiv paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2704.12345 (Sparse-KV-Mem)
  - Blog post on lowbit -> https://mlops.blog/lowbit-drift-2027
  - Kernel batching PR (internal): https://github.com/redwood-inference/pr/kernel-batching-proposal
  - Slack convo: #eng-inference thread "kv-prefetch-proposal" (link above)

Notes-to-self at end: keep this short and experiment-driven. Prioritize the replay experiment; it's the lowest lift and gives a measurable signal. When writing the Optimize recommendation, include a tiny checklist: workload length distribution, few-shot prompt templates, guardrail for hallucination regression.

End of scratchpad.
